R01-B-01: When a person who keeps all her appointments in a phone loses the phone, she often says that she has lost her memory, and the phrase is less of an exaggeration than it sounds. For a growing number of thinkers, the boundary of the mind is not the skin or the skull but the reach of the processes that do a mind's work. If a notebook is consulted as automatically as recollection, trusted as fully and available as readily, then, the argument goes, the information it holds is as much a part of its owner's beliefs as anything stored in the brain. To insist otherwise is, on this view, a mere prejudice in favour of the inside. The argument has real force, and much of it should be accepted. It is hard to say what principled difference there is between a fact that I must work to recall and a fact that I can retrieve, with less effort, from a list I always carry. Both are stored, both are retrieved, and both guide what I do. Ordinary practice already reflects this: we hold someone responsible for knowing what is written in the diary she relies on, and we speak of a shopping list as remembering things for us. When a skill depends on a tool, as a carpenter's feel for the wood depends on a plane he has used for years, the tool can seem less an object he handles than a part of how he perceives. Yet the stronger conclusion, that the mind simply is whatever system includes the tool, moves too quickly. Devices differ from memory in a way the argument tends to pass over: they can be edited by other people. A notebook can be altered while its owner sleeps; the contents of a phone can be changed by whoever manages the service on which it depends. Biological memory is fallible, and it too can be distorted by suggestion, but it is not open in the same routine way to the revisions of strangers. The difference is not one of storage but of authority, of who has the standing to change what a person takes to be true. The better lesson, then, is not that minds are everywhere but that trust has become a part of cognition. Once we lean on external stores, the question of whether our beliefs are sound becomes partly a question about the institutions and people who maintain those stores. That is why the loss, or the quiet alteration, of a device can feel like an injury to the self and not merely an inconvenience. The thesis that the mind extends into its tools is right to notice the injury; it is wrong to think that calling the device a part of the mind explains it.
R01-B-02: A man resolves to give up sweets, believes sincerely that he should, and then, at the end of a long and exhausting day, eats the cake anyway. The episode is so ordinary that its strangeness is easy to miss. If he really judged that refusing was better, what moved him to do otherwise? One very old answer is that nothing did: no one knowingly chooses the worse course, and the man must have ceased to believe, at least temporarily, that refusing was better. Most people find this answer too clever by half. They are convinced that they have acted against their own considered judgement, and they describe the experience in the vocabulary of force, of being overcome by something stronger than resolution. The popular picture that develops from this description treats the will as a kind of muscle. Judgement indicates the direction, and the will either possesses the strength to follow or it does not; lapses are failures of strength, to be corrected by training, rest or improved nutrition. The picture has the merit of matching how lapses feel, and it explains why they cluster at the end of tiring days. But it makes the lapse strangely external to the person, as though desire were a weight imposed from outside and the self merely a lifter who happened to be exhausted that particular evening. Closer examination of such moments suggests a different interpretation. The man with the cake does not usually go on thinking, clearly and vividly, that he should refuse while his hand reaches out. Instead his attention narrows: the considerations favouring refusal, which seemed compelling in the morning, become abstract and distant, while the cake is immediate, particular and present. He does not abandon his judgement so much as stop looking at it. On this interpretation the lapse is neither a mere deficiency of strength nor a simple change of mind but a failure to keep one's own reasons in view. This does not mean that fatigue is irrelevant, or that every lapse is a matter of attention; some temptations are simply strong, and some people are considerably more depleted than others. But the attentional account has a practical advantage. If lapses were exclusively failures of strength, the only remedy would be additional strength. If they are often failures of attention, the remedy can be arrangement: keeping one's reasons concrete, placing the cake out of sight, deciding in advance what one will do when the moment arrives. People who manage their weaknesses successfully tend to do precisely this, and the muscle picture has trouble explaining why such strategies work.
R01-B-03: The traditional problem of other minds begins from an asymmetry. I am aware of my own pain directly, the argument runs, but I know of yours only through what you do: the wince, the cry, the hand withdrawn abruptly from the stove. How, then, am I entitled to believe that anything lies behind your behaviour at all? The classic reply is an argument from analogy. In my own case I observe that pain is regularly accompanied by wincing and crying; when I observe wincing and crying in you, I infer that pain is present in you as well, concealed from me but similar to my own. Critics have long pointed out how fragile this inference is. It generalises from a single case to every other person, which is the kind of reasoning we would reject anywhere else: nobody who had examined one seed from a sack and found it fertile would conclude with any confidence that every seed in the sack would germinate. Worse, the conclusion can never be independently checked. In ordinary induction I can at least test a generalisation against further cases, but I can never step into your experience to confirm that the pain I inferred is really there. These objections are sound, but they share the assumption they attack: that knowledge of other minds must be an inference from bodily movements to concealed inner states. That assumption does not describe how such knowledge actually arises. A child does not first register a contraction of facial muscles and then hypothesise distress; she sees that her mother is upset, and she sees it as immediately as she sees that the cup is full. Expressions are not evidence from which feelings are deduced. They are, in a great many cases, the very form in which feelings are visible to others, and to treat them as mere outward signs is to describe the face as a mask before asking what lies behind it. None of this shows that we never reason about other minds. When a stranger's expressions are unfamiliar, when someone is deliberately concealing what she feels, or when we ask whether an octopus or a newborn experiences pain, we do weigh evidence and draw conclusions, and we can be badly wrong. But these are special cases, and they are intelligible only against a background in which most minds are simply seen. The sceptic's mistake is to take the hard case as the model for every case, and then to wonder why the model will not support the confidence we ordinarily have.
R01-B-04: For a long time emotions were cast as the adversaries of reason, surges of feeling that cloud judgement and must be governed by it. A more recent and considerably more flattering view inverts this picture. Emotions, it holds, are themselves judgements, or are at least constructed around them. To be afraid of a dog is to judge that the dog is dangerous; to feel indignant is to regard oneself as having been treated unjustly. The view has an obvious appeal. It explains why emotions can be appropriate or inappropriate to their circumstances, why we can sometimes argue a friend out of her jealousy by showing her that she has misread a situation, and why emotions are directed at objects rather than being mere sensations, like an itch or a cramp, that are about nothing at all. The difficulty arises from emotions that persist against judgement. A traveller may know perfectly well that flying is far safer than the drive to the airport, may say so and sincerely believe it, and still grip the armrest in terror as the aircraft climbs. If fear were a judgement that flying is dangerous, the traveller would be simultaneously affirming and denying the same proposition, and her condition would be a straightforward contradiction. Yet it does not feel like a contradiction, nor do we treat it as one; we recognise it as a familiar kind of inner conflict, unpleasant but not absurd. A better model is perception. When two lines of equal length are drawn with arrowheads pointing in opposite directions, one continues to look longer even after a ruler has shown that they are equal. Seeing is not believing, so the conflict involves no contradiction. Emotions, on this model, are something like perceptions of value: fear presents the climbing aircraft as dangerous in the way the illusion presents one line as longer. Such presentations are usually reliable and usually agree with our considered views, which is why the judgement theory seemed so plausible. When they disagree, we have the emotional counterpart of an optical illusion. The analogy should not be pressed too far. We do not blame anyone for seeing the lines as unequal, but we do sometimes criticise people for their fears and resentments, and we expect them to work on them. This suggests that emotions, unlike most perceptions, are partly answerable to the person who has them: they can be reshaped over time through reflection and repeated experience, even if they cannot be dismissed by a single act of judgement. The perceptual model explains why emotional conflict is not contradiction; it must be supplemented to explain why it is nevertheless an occasion for responsibility.
R01-B-05: A long tradition in philosophy, going back at least to Locke, holds that what makes me the same person as some earlier individual is neither the persistence of my body nor that of some hidden soul but memory. I am the person who sat that examination twenty years ago because I can remember sitting it, from the inside, as something I did. The view has an attractive modesty. It ties personal identity to something we actually experience rather than to an unobservable substance, and it appears to match our intuitions about imaginary cases: if all of my memories were somehow transferred into another body, many people feel that it is I who would wake up in it. The theory faces two well-known difficulties. The first concerns chains of memory. Imagine a woman of eighty who vividly remembers her first day as a teacher at thirty, and suppose that the teacher of thirty could still recall a childhood accident at six of which the woman of eighty remembers nothing. On a strict memory criterion the old woman is the teacher and the teacher is the child, yet the old woman is not the child, since she remembers nothing of her. Identity cannot behave this way: if A is the same as B and B is the same as C, then A is the same as C. The second difficulty is subtler. To distinguish a genuine memory of sitting an examination from a vivid but false impression of having sat it, we seem to need to know already that the rememberer is the person who sat it. Memory, apparently, presupposes the identity it was supposed to explain. The first objection can be met by allowing overlapping chains of memory, rather than direct memory, to carry identity; the second is much harder to escape. Yet it is worth asking what the defenders of the memory view were really after. Their deepest conviction was not a thesis about the logic of identity but a claim about what makes the past matter to a person. A past that I can recall, whose intentions I have carried out and whose anxieties still shape me, is mine in a way that a past I share only bodily is not. Seen in this light, the theory fails as an account of identity and succeeds as an account of something else: the degree to which a person is connected to her own history. That connection comes in degrees and can weaken, which identity, being all or nothing, cannot do. The old woman is the child she once was, but she is far less connected to that child than to the teacher. Many of our practical concerns, from the keeping of old promises to the sense of responsibility for what we did long ago, may track this connection more closely than they track identity itself.
R01-B-06: Philosophical discussions of ethics characteristically concentrate on the moment of decision. A situation is described, the available options are set out, and the question is which of them a good person would choose. This framing is natural for the purposes of argument, but it quietly assumes that the morally significant work begins only once the situation has been described. In ordinary life, nobody hands us the description. What we take the situation to be, which features stand out and which recede into the background, is settled largely by what we attend to, and that settling is accomplished before any choice is considered. Consider a manager who prides herself on her fairness. When a request for leave arrives, she weighs it conscientiously against the requirements of the team, and she applies identical rules to everyone. Yet for months she has failed to notice that one reserved employee has grown withdrawn and anxious, while she registered immediately when a more assertive colleague appeared dissatisfied. Her decisions, examined individually, may be beyond reproach. The defect lies upstream, in a pattern of attention that has made some people's difficulties vivid to her and rendered others' invisible. It may be objected that this demands too much of ordinary moral agents. Noticing is not something we do at will; we cannot be blamed for failing to perceive what never came to our notice, any more than for failing to hear a sound pitched too high for human ears. There is something genuinely correct in the objection. No single lapse of attention is a choice, and it would be unjust to treat it as though it were. But attention is not fixed in the way the range of hearing is. It is formed by what we have habitually looked for, by whom we have taken seriously, and by the stories we tell ourselves about the people around us, and these are things over which, across time, we have considerable influence. The upshot is that moral improvement is frequently less a matter of resolving to choose better than of learning to see better. A person who wishes to be fair must ask not only whether her decisions follow sound principles but also whose circumstances reach her as calls for decision at all. This is slower and less dramatic work than heroic choice, and it rarely earns admiration, since what it changes is largely invisible from outside. It is nonetheless where a great deal of moral life actually takes place.
R01-B-07: Arguments about free will customarily proceed in a fixed order. First we are asked to settle a question about the world: whether every event, including every human choice, is determined by antecedent causes. Only then, it is assumed, can we know whether anyone is genuinely responsible for anything, and therefore whether blame and praise are ever deserved. If the causal question is answered one way, our practices of holding one another responsible are vindicated; if it is answered the other way, those practices are exposed as resting on an illusion, and intellectual honesty requires us to abandon them. An influential alternative reverses this order. It begins not with metaphysics but with the attitudes we actually adopt toward one another: resentment when we are injured through someone's indifference, gratitude when we are helped through their goodwill, indignation on behalf of others who have been mistreated. These attitudes, the alternative maintains, are not conclusions derived from a theory about causation. They are constitutive of what it is to live among persons rather than merely alongside objects, and to suppose that a philosophical thesis could oblige us to relinquish them is to misunderstand both the thesis and ourselves. We do suspend them in particular cases: when someone acted under duress, or did not know what he was doing, or is a young child. But these suspensions are made within the practice, for reasons the practice itself recognises, and none of them amounts to a general verdict on human agency. There is much to admire in this reversal. It explains why the free will debate so often seems unreal to people outside it, who continue resenting and forgiving whatever the latest argument concludes, and it rightly insists that responsibility is something we do together rather than a concealed property awaiting detection. Responsibility, on this picture, resembles a language more than a fact of nature: it is sustained by shared expectations, and its rules are learned by taking part in it. The reversal also shows why the most sweeping sceptical arguments overreach: from the bare claim that choices have causes, nothing follows about whether a particular person was acting under duress, or in ignorance, or as a child acts. Yet the reversal is sometimes taken to establish more than it can. If the practice is answerable only to itself, it may seem immune to criticism, and its present configuration may seem beyond question. The history of the practice tells against such complacency. Over time, many societies have come to regard certain compulsions, illnesses and conditions of upbringing as diminishing responsibility where they were formerly treated as plain wickedness. These revisions were not imposed by metaphysics; they arose when people learned more about how particular capacities can fail, and then applied excusing principles the practice already contained to cases it had previously judged harshly. This is where the sciences of the mind may matter after all, though not in the way the traditional debate supposed. No general thesis about determinism will tell us whether blame is ever deserved. But detailed findings about how self-control develops, or how it is impaired, can reveal that the conditions our practice already counts as excusing are more common, or less conspicuous, than we had assumed. A discovery that some apparent callousness is in fact an inability to register the distress of others, for instance, would not refute the practice; it would require the practice to be consistent with itself. The practice of holding responsible is neither a fixed point beyond inquiry nor a conclusion awaiting metaphysical proof. It is a body of standards that can be held to its own commitments, and inquiry into the mind is one of the ways in which that is done.
R01-B-08: It has become a commonplace, in philosophy as much as in popular psychology, that a self is a kind of story. On this view a person is not a thing that persists beneath her experiences but the narrative she composes from them: the account of where she came from, what she has struggled against and where she is heading. The claim is usually advanced in two forms at once. The descriptive form says that human beings do in fact understand themselves through stories. The normative form adds that they ought to, and that a life which cannot be gathered into a coherent narrative is in some way impoverished or broken. The descriptive claim is plausible for many people, but its generality is doubtful. Some people report that they do not experience their lives as a plot at all. They feel little connection with the person they were a decade ago, find the invitation to tell their life story faintly baffling, and live with their attention fixed on present tasks and relationships. Nor is there any obvious sense in which their lives go worse: they form attachments, deliberate carefully and take responsibility for their conduct, only without experiencing their existence as an unfolding plot. It would be rash to assume that such people are simply unreflective, or that they are concealing a narrative they would rather not acknowledge. Their testimony is at least as credible as that of people who say the opposite, and it suggests that narrative self-understanding is one way of being a self rather than the condition of being one. The normative claim is more troubling. Stories have shapes, and the pressure to give one's life a shape is a pressure to select. Episodes that fit the arc are remembered and retold; those that do not are discarded or reinterpreted. Autobiographical memory is already reconstructive, and a governing narrative supplies it with a principle of selection that is rarely examined. A person who has told herself for years that she is someone who overcomes adversity will find it difficult to see the occasions on which she gave up, and harder still to learn from them. The demand for coherence can thus become a demand for a flattering kind of forgetting. A novelist may legitimately omit whatever does not serve the plot; a life conducted on the same principle may lose precisely the evidence it most needs. None of this means that narrative has no place. Making a promise requires regarding one's future self as continuous with one's present intention, and recovering from bereavement or injury often involves finding a way to tell what happened so that it can be lived with. Understanding other people, too, frequently depends on grasping the story they take themselves to be in. These are genuine goods, and a person who could never assemble any part of her past into an account would be at a real disadvantage. But the goods enumerated here are those of an instrument, not of an essence. We use stories to bind ourselves, to heal and to understand, and we can use them well or badly, often or seldom. To say that the self simply is its story makes the instrument indispensable, and it turns a difference in temperament into a deficiency. The more modest view leaves room both for lives that are lived largely in the present and for the episodes that refuse to fit, and it may well be the more truthful of the two.
